html:
In 1543 a Chinese junk with Portuguese traders aboard landed on Tanegashima, a small island south of Kyushu, and the Portuguese showed the local lord their matchlock guns. He bought two and had his smiths copy them.

Within a few decades Japanese workshops were making matchlocks, called tanegashima after the island, in large numbers. They arrived in the middle of the Sengoku period, a century of war between rival lords, and changed how battles were fought. Oda Nobunaga used massed gunners against the Takeda cavalry at the Battle of Nagashino in 1575, and castles grew thick stone walls.

The guns came with the first Europeans in Japan. Portuguese ships soon traded regularly, and Francis Xavier began Christian missions in 1549. Firearms helped the three unifiers, Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu, end the civil wars. In the long peace of Tokugawa Japan guns mattered much less, though they never vanished.
